IGP ordered to purge police force of corrupt officials. LAHORE: Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz has ordered the inspector general of police (IGP) to purge the force of “corrupt officials” within a week. Presiding over a meeting on law and order here on Tuesday, the chief minister said maintaining peace and protecting the lives and property of citizens remained the government’s top priority. The chief minister said police officers known for corruption should not be appointed as station house officers (SHOs) and called for strict action against corrupt officials. She also directed the police to intensify efforts to curb burglary and ordered a clean-up operation in Sheikhupura to eliminate crime. The CM decided to bring the operational control of Dolphin Police under the jurisdiction of the respective police stations. She also set Sept 30 deadline for equipping Punjab Police personnel with body cameras. She sought a comprehensive plan to ensure effective control of crimes against women and children and ordered a zero-tolerance policy against those involved in such offences. She also approved the installation of GPS devices and cameras in prisoner vans and directed the authorities to take strict action over incidents involving the escape of prisoners. The meeting was told that the overall crime situation in the province had improved, with robberies declining by 54 per cent, murders by 35pc, car snatching by 46pc and motorcycle theft by 53pc. The chief minister said district police officers would be held accountable in districts where crime rates remained high. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

Deadline for online registration of arms dealers’ data extended. LAHORE: Punjab home department has extended the deadline for arms dealers by 10 days to upload all required information on the online digital inventory registration system. The deadline for registering the existing stock and records of all purchases and sales has now been set for Sept 6, 2026. All arms dealers will be required to register their complete stocks and sale-purchase records on the online portal by the stipulated date. A department spokesman says that complete records of all firearms and ammunition held by each arms dealer will be available on the home department’s online portal, along with details of their purchase and sale transactions. Out of a total 413 registered arms dealers in the province, 230 have already entered their details in the digital inventory system, the spokesman says. All deputy commissioners (DC) are assisting arms dealers in their respective districts in the registration of their digital inventories. The decision to extend the deadline was taken at a training workshop organised by home department for arms dealers in Lahore, to provide them guidance on the digital inventory registration system on Tuesday. Over 350 arms dealers, including those online, participated in the workshop from the offices of the DCs concerned to get themselves acquainted with the digital inventory registration system on the Punjab Arms Licence Portal. The spokesperson says the online registration of arms stocks and purchase and sale transactions is aimed at eliminating crime from Punjab and curbing the illegal purchase and sale of arms. “The arms dealers failing to upload their inventories will face legal action, besides suspension of their licenses, sealing of their businesses, and fines imposed in accordance with the law,” the spokesman says. Home department Additional Secretary (Judicial) Abdul Rauf, Deputy Secretary (Judicial) Muhammad Murtaza and National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra) officials provided training to the arms dealers on the use of the online portal and registration of digital inventories during the workshop. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

Mayor Mamdani opposes NYC event with leader of India's Hindu nationalist group. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said on Tuesday he did not support an upcoming event in his city featuring the leader of the Hindu nationalist group that is the ideological parent of India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Mohan Bhagwat, chief of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), is scheduled to speak at a Manhattan event on Saturday, according to the event’s website. “I don’t support the rally, but I don’t know if the city has any jurisdiction on cancelling a private event,” Mamdani, who is the first Muslim and Indian American mayor of New York City, said when asked if the event should be cancelled. “The vision of India that I was taught by my family and one that I grew up being very familiar with was of a pluralistic society of a secular Republic that believed in the belonging of each and every person who was from India. And it has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision.” The event’s website casts the August 29 gathering as the “Universal Oneness Celebration” bringing together the Hindu American community. The organisers, American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue, say the event is backed by several Hindu American groups and promotes shared heritage and interfaith unity. Many local organisations have criticised it over Bhagwat’s attendance and the RSS’ history. The RSS, a powerful Hindu group from which Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s BJP emerged, said in May it had organised foreign visits, including to the US, to counter perceptions it is a paramilitary outfit involved in attacks on minority communities. The US Commission on International Religious Freedom says the RSS “has been involved in acts of extreme violence and intolerance against members of minority groups for decades”. The RSS disputes intolerance accusations and says it is a “Hindu-centric civilisational, cultural movement” whose goal is to “carry the nation to the pinnacle of glory”, including by uniting Hindus. United Nations and human rights groups say abuse of Indian minorities has risen in recent years, pointing to rising hate speeches , a religion-based citizenship law , the demolition of Muslim-owned properties, the removal of occupied Kashmir’s autonomy and an anti-conversion legislation that challenges freedom of belief. The BJP-led Indian government denies being discriminatory and says its policies, including food subsidy programmes and electrification drives, benefit all communities.

Pakistan captain Babar Azam returns against England '90pc fit'. Pakistan captain Babar Azam on Wednesday said he is “90 per cent fit” as he returns to lead his country in the second Test against England at Lord’s. Azam missed last week’s series opener at Headingley because of a finger injury, with the tourists thrashed by an innings and 103 runs in his absence as England went 1-0 up in a three-match campaign. The 31-year-old Azam was hit on the glove while batting during a warm-up match, compounding a finger injury initially sustained during Pakistan’s recent tour of the West Indies. But he has been back batting in the nets during the past 48 hours and the experienced batsman is now set to strengthen a Pakistan side dismissed for just 171 and 135 in Leeds when the second Test gets underway on Thursday. “I’ve had a couple of practice sessions again, and I’m 90 per cent fit for the match tomorrow,” Azam told a pre-match press conference at Lord’s. “Always when you lead the Pakistan team, especially at this ground, it is an honour for me and I will do my best. If it is on the field as captain or when I’m batting, I will just play my game.” He added: “I think we were not playing up to our mark [in the first Test], but credit to England for the way they are playing. After that we sat to discuss our mistakes and now we are looking forward to the match, believing in ourselves and we will try to play good cricket.” Azam was Pakistan’s top run-scorer in the West Indies, with 193 runs during a drawn two-Test series. He has also enjoyed success in England, with three fifties in six innings while averaging 65.75. Azan Awais may make way if Azam returns at number four, with either Shan Masood or Abdullah Shafique moving up the order to open. Pakistan could also make changes to their bowling line-up as well this week, with 20-year-old Ubaid Shah able to provide extra speed to an attack lacking in sheer pace in Leeds. That would leave Khurram Shahzad and Mohammad Ali vying for one place, with Mohammad Abbas the most reliable of Pakistan’s pacemen at Headingley and left-arm spinner Ali Usman fresh from his maiden five-wicket haul in Test cricket.

Bill Gates warns world dangerously unprepared for AI upheaval. Bill Gates warned on Wednesday that the world is dangerously unprepared for the upheaval brought by artificial intelligence, with the technology destroying jobs and threatening human connection, especially for young people. In a nearly 6,000-word essay published on his blog, the Microsoft co-founder said the shift into the AI era will rank among the most turbulent periods in human history and that no one has produced a credible plan for managing it. His stance will draw significant pushback from many in Silicon Valley and the Trump administration who blame “doomer” attitudes among some tech leaders for giving the AI revolution a bad reputation. “AI will either be the greatest equaliser ever invented, or the worst source of injustice,” wrote Gates, 70, who now chairs the philanthropic foundation that bears his name. “There is no plan to ease the entry into the AI era,” Gates said, adding that he would likely support one if it existed. “However, I don’t think that’s going to happen. The geopolitical and economic incentives are pushing too hard to go full speed ahead,” he warned. Gates said he saw three main risks arising from the fast deployment of AI. The first is permanent job destruction. Gates insisted comparisons to the shift from farm work to office work were misleading, as that transition unfolded over generations and created roles that still required human thinking. AI can substitute for thinking itself, he warned, hitting law, medicine, customer service, software and manufacturing within roughly a decade. Entry- and mid-level positions are the most exposed, Gates said, leaving young people entering a labour market with far fewer openings. Blue-collar work will follow as robots become cheaper, with the construction and hospitality sectors feeling pressure by the end of the decade. Gates suggested that some jobs should be set aside for humans, even if AI can do them better and more cheaply. The second risk is that AI hands new capabilities to bad actors. Gates said cybersecurity specialists he knows are alarmed that attackers are gaining ground faster than defenders can patch weaknesses. Hospitals, banks, water systems and power grids are all exposed, he said. The third area of risk concerns children and human relationships. Citing research, Gates said AI chatbots that never challenge or frustrate users risk becoming addictive and deny people the chance to build social skills. AI bots “rob us of the lessons we learn from connecting with other people,” he wrote. Gates acknowledged he retains deep financial ties to the technology industry, saying investment profits will flow to his foundation, which plans to spend its remaining $200 billion over the next two decades. The essay comes months after Gates was interviewed by the House Oversight Committee over his ties to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, telling lawmakers in June that the association was “a grave error in judgment”.

Centre, AJK govt to work with other parties to build consensus on governance, constitutional issues: Dar. Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar said the Centre and the incoming Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) government would work with other political parties and stakeholders to form consensus on “important governance and constitutional issues”, it emerged on Wednesday. Dar’s statement came as he discussed recent developments in AJK with a group of cross-party Pakistan-origin British parliamentarians at Pakistan House in London, Foreign Office (FO) said in a statement on Wednesday. Dar held the meeting as part of his five-day official visit to the United Kingdom, which began on Monday. The parliamentarians included Lord Zameer Choudrey , Lord Qurban Hussain, Baroness Shaista Sheehan, and Lord Shaffaq Mohammed, as well as Members of Parliament Mohammad Yasin, Yasmin Qureshi, Afzal Khan, Zubir Ahmed and Adnan Hussain. The British parliamentarians congratulated DPM Dar on PML-N’s victory in the recent AJK elections , the FO noted. Dar said the people of AJK had “reposed their confidence in the PML-N because of its past record of delivering economic growth and development”. “He said the new government would prioritise investment in infrastructure and job creation for the youth of Azad Jammu and Kashmir,” FO said in its statement. Lawmaker Imran Hussain said on X that he “made strong representations to British government ministers that the concerns of more than one million British Kashmiris about the ongoing situation in Kashmir must be raised first and foremost”. “Reports of bloodshed, arbitrary arrests, restrictions on communications and disruption to essential supplies must be raised directly and seriously with Pakistan, and directly with their deputy prime minister,” he added. Ahead of the general elections in AJK, unrest grew in the region as the regional administration and the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) were at odds over various issues, most notably the committee’s demand to abolish the 12 seats in the region’s Legislative Assembly, which resulted in protests across the region. On June 5, the JAAC was declared a proscribed organisation by the regional government and placed under the First Schedule of the region’s anti-terrorism act (ATA). On Saturday, outgoing AJK Prime Minister Faisal Mumtaz Rathore said the biggest challenge for the incoming government was dealing with the JAAC, stressing that dialogue was the only way to resolve the crisis. In his meeting, Dar also “appreciated the important role played by the British parliamentarians in strengthening Pakistan-UK ties and their staunch advocacy for a just settlement of the Jammu and Kashmir dispute”. “The parliamentarians shared their views on other matters of common interest and reaffirmed their commitment to further cementing ties between Pakistan and the UK,” FO said. The British lawmakers further lauded Pakistan’s mediation efforts in the US-Israeli war on Iran . “They said that Pakistan’s historic role had been internationally recognised and had filled all overseas Pakistanis with pride.” DPM Dar, in response, underscored that all parties adhering to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding was critical for “durable peace and stability in the region”. He also mentioned Pakistan’s Makkah Joint Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye as an important pact “in strengthening regional peace and stability”. Dar stressed that the agreement was “purely defensive in nature”, FO said.

Hina Javed murder case: Rawalpindi court extends physical remand of suspects for another 3 days. RAWALPINDI: A duty magistrate on Wednesday extended the physical remand of Hina Javed’s husband and domestic servant for another three days for further investigation into her murder case. Javed, a 45-year-old digital media executive, was found dead with her hands tied behind her back at an apartment in Rawalpindi last Thursday. Police said the body bore signs of torture and formed a special investigation team, detaining her husband and domestic servant while also questioning her father-in-law as part of the investigation. The suspects were produced before the court of Duty Magistrate Rana Shah Nawaz after the completion of a three-day remand handed to them earlier. The police requested seven more days of the suspects’ custody. However, the duty magistrate instead extended the physical remand by another three days for further investigation. Shah Khawar, the advocate counsel for the family of the deceased, told the media after court proceedings that the investigation was proceeding in the right direction, as the police had collected evidence and conducted a forensic examination. The victim’s “hyoid bone was broken and torture marks” were found on her body by the doctor who conducted the postmortem examination on her body after obtaining swab, saliva and blood samples for analysis by the Punjab Forensic Science Agency (PFSA). A complete postmortem report, describing the cause of her death and other details, will be submitted after the PFSA analysis report is received. On Tuesday, the special investigating team formed to investigate the murder moved the suspects to Lahore for a DNA and polygraph test amid tight security. A polygraph test, also known as a lie detector test, is used by the police as a tool to help investigate crimes or clear suspects. After the test, the suspects were taken back to Rawalpindi and produced before the duty magistrate’s court on Wednesday. Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) Operations Tariq Mehboob also recorded the statements of the two suspects. Both were said to disclose that the victim’s body was dragged into the bathroom and her neck tied with wire to stage a suicide, which was exposed when the police team arrived at the scene and collected evidence. Regional Police Officer Babar Sarfraz Alpa revealed to the media on Monday that the tragic incident took place on August 20. The police had initially received information that thieves had entered the house. When the police arrived, the victim’s body was partially hanging from a shower rod in the bathroom, he said. A first information report (FIR) was registered on Aug 20 at the Civil Lines police station under Sections 302 (premeditated murder) and 34 (common intention) of the Pakistan Penal Code on the complaint of Hina’s brother Fahad Javed. He alleged that his sister had been murdered by her husband, his father and their domestic servant.

US pauses immigrant visa applications worldwide: report. The Trump administration has paused immigrant visa applications worldwide to accommodate “in-depth training” for consular officers, as it seeks to screen out applicants deemed likely to need US assistance, The Financial Times ( FT ) reported on Tuesday. The move marks another step in the Trump administration’s signature drive to reduce immigration into the United States. Applicants with scheduled interviews at US embassies and consulates received emails saying their appointments were being rescheduled and that they would receive notice of new dates and times. “A more prosperous America means ensuring that visa applicants are not likely to become a public charge, as defined under US law and regulation, and not likely to become dependent on US public benefits reserved for qualified Americans in need,” a State Department spokesperson told the FT . The department this month launched “a global training initiative” to “ensure all consular officers are fully equipped to evaluate every visa applicant comprehensively and consistently,” the spokesperson said. Brian Simmons, senior US consular manager at immigration law firm Fragomen in Washington, said many affected applicants had “already spent thousands of dollars and disrupted their lives to attend scheduled interviews, only to have their appointments cancelled at the last minute”. The State Department did not say when appointments would resume, saying: “To accommodate this in-depth training, appointments for visa services will be adjusted.” A privilege, not a right The US government plans to revoke the visas of foreigners who came to the country for tourism or business but sought to stay longer by applying for asylum, the State Department said on Tuesday. The administration said it is now working with the Department of Homeland Security to identify and revoke the visas of people who, it said, came to America billing themselves as temporary visitors but then applied for asylum so they could stay permanently. “Obtaining a visa in order to seek asylum is fraud — which is grounds for visa revocation,” State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in a statement that confirmed press reports about the new policy. The White House, in a post on X, suggested “up to two hundred thousand visas” would be affected and claimed it would be the “largest mass visa revocation in history”. The State Department neither confirmed nor denied that number. Pigott said, “The number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis.” Early this month, the department said that since President Donald Trump returned to power in January 2025, some 175,000 foreigners had seen their US visas revoked on grounds ranging from criminal offences, including driving under the influence, to praising the killing of the right-wing activist Charlie Kirk. The administration also recently revoked the visas of Mexican officials, including the son of the former president Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador. This prompted a complaint from the current president, Claudia Sheinbaum. Trump, who won reelection in large part on his promise to fight illegal immigration, has expelled huge numbers of people who were in the country without proper residence papers. But he has also worked to restrict the entry of foreigners who do go by the rules and has gone after those who overstay their visas after they expire. Some of these measures have been challenged and curtailed by the courts. Last Friday, a federal judge struck down a government ban on visas to nationals from 75 countries who wish to settle in the country indefinitely. These countries included Afghanistan, Brazil, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Nigeria, Somalia, Thailand and Yemen. The Trump administration is also planning to expand vetting of the social media accounts of visa applicants. “We are making clear that a visa is a privilege — not a right,” Pigott said on Tuesday.

GB to auction hunting permits for 3 markhors, 14 blue sheep, 100 ibexes. GILGIT: Gilgit-Baltistan’s Parks and Wildlife Department will auction hunting permits for three Astore markhor, 14 blue sheep and 100 ibexes for the GB Trophy Hunting programme 2026-27. The highest permit base rate is for markhor, set at $200,000. The base rate for blue sheep hunting permits has been set at $25,000, and at $11,000 for Himalayan ibex. The auction notice said that out of the exportable quota of four Astore markhors, one permit had been extended from the last hunting season, so three new permits would be auctioned in September. The open bidding for the permits will be held on September 10 at the Forest Complex in Jutial, Gilgit. According to the official notice, trophy hunting will be conducted under GB Trophy Hunting Guidelines 2019, starting October 15 until April 10, 2027. Hunting would be permissible only in the designated conservation areas. The trophy hunting quota had been set on the basis of annual surveys conducted by wildlife experts, the notice said. GB Chief Conservator Parks and Wildlife Zakir Hussain told Dawn that last year, Rs350 million was collected from the auctioned permits against a target of Rs550m. He added that permits for two Astore markhors, five blue sheep and 10 exportable Himalayan ibexes went unused in the 2025-26 trophy hunting programme, resulting in a loss of Rs200m . Hussain had told Dawn at the time that the law and order situation following violent protests in Gilgit and Skardu — against the assassination of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in US-Israeli attacks — had led to the cancellation of hunting plans by American and other foreign hunters. Local business owners and tour operators have been opposing the permit rate hikes for the past two years, claiming that the decision had damaged their businesses and discouraged international clients. They have warned of losses for businesses and the local communities who rely on trophy-hunting revenue. Ikram Beg, a business owner who sells hunting equipment, said the trophy hunting conservation programme in GB was facing a serious challenge. “Over the last two years, the Wildlife Department has repeatedly increased trophy hunting baseline price by more than 300 per cent without adequately considering the recommendations of key stakeholders,” he said. Beg said that the unilateral and excessive increases were making GB less competitive in the international hunting market. He warned that if the trend continued, it could reduce hunting revenue, weaken community incentives and ultimately put the entire conservation programme at risk. “Trophy hunting was introduced as a conservation tool, not simply as a means of maximising government revenue. Its success depends on sustainable pricing, international participation, transparent management and meaningful benefits for local communities,” he noted. Local business owners demanded that the relevant authorities review and rationalise baseline prices as well as consult communities, conservation experts and professional stakeholders, while ensuring transparency and compliance with relevant regulations and requirements. Despite global controversy surrounding trophy hunting, supporters argue that such programmes help prevent poaching, empower local communities and contribute to wildlife conservation. Hunting the three animals is extremely challenging in the region, with hunters facing rugged, difficult slopes and extremely cold weather. The trophy hunting programme started in GB with the local community’s involvement in Bar Valley, Nagar, in 1990. Around 80pc of the money earned from licences goes to the community for wildlife protection and conservation. Last year, the GB Wildlife and Parks Department had auctioned off hunting permits for 118 animals for the 2025–26 season, with the top permit for an Astore markhor fetching $370,000. GB is rich in biodiversity due to its varied climate and ecosystems. The region is home to several rare species, including Marco Polo sheep, ibex, markhor, urial, blue sheep, lynx, snow leopard, leopard cat, brown and black bears, wolves, foxes, marmots, chakor, ram chakor and golden eagles. However, many of these species face threats from illegal hunting, wildlife mismanagement and climate change.

Team unable to locate Pakistani climber Asma Mushtaq's body on Spantik after hours-long efforts. A recovery team has descended back to Camp 2 from the spot on Gilgit-Baltistan’s Spantik Peak where the body of deceased Pakistani climber Asma Mushtaq was suspected to be buried under the snow, an official said. The 34-year-old climber died on Aug 20 while descending from the mountain, also known as Golden Peak, after suffering from high-altitude sickness. Her body was said to be at Camp 3, which is located at a height of approximately 6,250 metres. Alpine Club of Pakistan (ACP) General Secretary Ayaz Shigri told Dawn that the six-member team reached Camp 3 on Wednesday, where the body was suspected to be. However, he added, the team could not find the body after several hours of intense search. He said it was unclear whether the team would continue their search on Thursday or delay the mission, stressing the weather’s importance. Shigri said it was feared that the climber’s body was buried under snow after the peak received fresh snowfall, adding that there were also high winds at the peak. Highlighting that the six-member local team consists of highly professional climbers, Shigri said Pakistan Army helicopters were expected to airlift Mushtaq’s body to Skardu after its arrival at the base camp. The ACP member pointed out that helicopters could not retrieve the body from altitudes over 6,000m. “Only the ground rescue team can bring down the body from the peak to base camp,” he emphasised. In a post on social media earlier, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar also noted that as the “place is very large and due to heavy snowfall over the past two days, the body is now completely covered under the snow, making it difficult to locate”. According to the minister, the rescue team’s search efforts had been ongoing for two hours as of around 4pm. The team had resumed its search operation on Tuesday once weather conditions improved, after heavy snowfall had halted the retrieval efforts on Sunday. During her ascent, Mushtaq had successfully reached the 7,027-metre summit of Spantik and was in good health at the time, the ACP said in statements issued on Thursday. However, she developed a serious high-altitude medical emergency at an elevation of about 6,400 metres during the descent. High-altitude sickness encompasses a range of pulmonary and cerebral conditions caused by hypoxia, or oxygen deprivation, due to rapid ascent and inadequate acclimatisation to high altitudes. Shigri earlier told Dawn that Mushtaq was part of a five-member Pakistani women’s expedition team that summited Spantik, which included climbers Zoni Aslam, Zaba Shigri, Shama and Sohana. Climate change-induced shifts in weather patterns have worsened conditions on the peaks of the Karakoram Range in GB, creating serious difficulties for mountaineers. Body of US climber shifted to Islamabad Meanwhile, the body of US climber Sarah Mallory Geis was shifted to Islamabad on Wednesday for repatriation to her country, a day after it was airlifted to Skardu. ACP’s Shigri told Dawn that the body was dispatched via Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) from Skardu Airport on Wednesday morning. The body was received by an international insurance company that is responsible for its repatriation to her country. Geis was among the 10 mountaineers who lost their lives after being struck by an avalanche on Broad Peak (8,047 metres) last month. Her body was recovered from Broad Peak 22 days after she went missing in the deadly incident. Up until now, Geis was one of the last two climbers from the expedition whose bodies could not be retrieved. Earlier, Shigri said that the search for the last member of the expedition, Nawang Thindu Sherpa, was also under way.

Situationer: Unanswered questions linger hours after Pims fire tragedy. At around 4:30 pm, almost 10 hours after the fire that killed 14 infants, the entrance to the gynaecology ward at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Science (Pims) remained crowded. Eyewitnesses and relatives of victims had been hushed away hours ago, and the families left when the bodies were handed over. But there was an army of reporters and a line of cameramen set up in a neat row, waiting to see if anyone would show up. Everyone felt there was more to the story. The Mother Children Hospital (MCH) ward, situated at the western end of the healthcare facility, was sealed soon after the fire was reported. The main entrance at the north was also cordoned off with yellow tape, which has since been knocked down by the rush of people. To ensure the ward remained sealed, several policemen were posted at the gate, in addition to the hospital guards inside, apparently to ensure no daredevil reporter or cameraman was able to get inside. A bag of riot control gear, batons included, lay outside the entrance. For some strange reason, officials from the Punjab Highway Police prowled around the scene. Reporters and cameraman at the PIMS hospital in Islamabad hours after a fire killed 14 infants at the facility. — All photos by author A woman carrying a sick child was arguing with the policemen at the gate when I arrived. She held up the child and pleaded for several minutes until the guard inside finally relented and opened the gate just enough to let her in. As if on cue, a few reporters darted forward, but the door was swung shut again before they could get to it. Soon after, the reporters turned their attention towards a different source of commotion: a man started screaming and cameras gathered around. People in the crowd asked him if he had lost a child, but the man ignored the question. He simply exhorted the reporters that God would not forgive them if they didn’t go inside and report the truth of the matter. “They are martyrs,” he screamed before walking away. Rumours, denials The chatter was the same everywhere. Conflicting timelines, locked doors and whispers of coverups. Several people asked where exactly the nursery ward was located; most reporters and onlookers had never been inside the hospital. There was a general sense that no one truly knew what had happened. One person on the site confidently told me that the fire began due to a fault in the air conditioning system. Another said he knew for a fact there was a fault in the incubators. Rescue teams broke into the building by punching holes into the concrete grill and climbing though the window. — All images by author The only sign that a rescue operation had taken place here were some broken windows; a few by people before the rescue teams arrived. They said the bulk of the rescue was done by the people themselves. The fire brigade team that carried out the initial rescue had rotated out of their shift by 2pm. The new team sat on the ground next to a parked fire truck, even though the fire had long been extinguished. A member of the replacement team showed me the two places the building had been broken into. Firefighters had reached the site to find both the northern and western gates locked, he told me. Several people on the scene told me that locking the maternity ward was usual business; there is a fear of newborns being kidnapped. So the firefighters had set up ladders, broken two big holes into the building and carried out the initial rescue. Some said the fire brigade team only carried out adults stuck in the ward. The replacement firemen weren’t sure themselves. Journalist Qurrat-ul-AIn Shirazi showed me a video of a fireman bringing down a small wrapped body. “Everyone gives a different timeline, a different version,” she told me. Alina Shahid, a journalist, also told me that the rescue operation was wrapped up before 11am and the bodies handed over to the families. She also said eyewitnesses told her that the initial rescue operations were impeded. The bodies were moved to a mortuary, quickly identified and handed over soon after the operation ended. “They [families] were handed the bodies and hurried away from the scene,” a woman on the scene told me. “Everything seemed to be happening in a hurry.” Farah Rabbani, a journalist who had arrived at the site just after 9am, told me that she truly realised things were serious when she received a video from the Edhi rescue service showing small coffins being prepared. She was perhaps one of the few reporters who actually managed to get inside the ward. “It’s completely destroyed,” she told me, “floor to ceiling, everything is burnt.” The other entrance that had also been sealed is at the western end. There were no reporters gathered there so I decided to see for myself. A moment later, I realised why. That side of the building has an open corridor blocked only by a grill. And through that grill came what can only be described as the worst smell I have ever experienced: burnt plastic and charred flesh. The western entrance, which opens into a corridor, was deserted. All photos by author Questions remain Politicians came and went. Health Minister Mustafa Kamal had left minutes before I arrived. PPP’s Sherry Rehman had visited before him. Soon, leader of the opposition in the Senate, Allama Raja Nasir Abbas, appeared and took care to emphasise that not letting the media in was an attempt at a cover up. Minutes after he left, PPP’s Shahid Khattak was on the scene. The lines were repetitive; the questions remained. Had the bodies been identified? This was another question that elicited several confident responses. Some said the tags placed on the infants’ limbs were intact. Others said identification was still in process. None of the people who could actually answer the questions were on the scene anymore.

Iran-Oman talks on Strait of Hormuz: What we know. Iran and Oman are negotiating the opening of a temporary shipping corridor and the clearance of mines in the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, which both nations border. They have yet to agree on the conditions for the waterway’s reopening as the Middle East war nears the six-month mark, but talks are ongoing. Here’s what we know about the latest negotiations between Tehran and Muscat. Why Oman? Both countries sit on the strait crucial for the global oil and gas trade, and are trying to define the terms of a controlled resumption of shipping, which has been paralysed by Tehran since the US-Israeli attacks that started the war in late February. A Pakistan-mediated memorandum of understanding signed between the US and Iran in mid-June provided for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and left it up to Tehran and Muscat “to define the future administration and maritime services” in the waterway, in discussion with Gulf states and in line with international law. But the deal, which was supposed to pave the way for talks on permanently ending the war, has since fallen apart. Is there any progress? In Tehran on Tuesday, the Iranian and Omani foreign ministers discussed a framework agreement that would establish a “temporary corridor” for shipping and a project to clear mines in the strait, according to a joint statement. Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi said on X after the talks that he hoped the new corridor and “ practical arrangements to restore safe navigation” would be announced “soon”. He added that “future management of the strait and a permanent solution will follow in due course”. Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi, in an interview with local media, explained the proposed arrangement would see ships entering the Gulf pass through Iranian waters, while those leaving would use Omani waters. He also said that if the plan with Oman was agreed upon, the two would have 30 to 60 days to hammer out a permanent route, adding that Iran’s Revolutionary Guards were involved in the talks and that the maps under discussion were drawn up by the armed forces. The Guards said on Wednesday that they had agreed in negotiations with Oman to share revenues earned from any fees imposed in the strait — an idea rejected by Washington. Why are talks held up? Tehran continues to make the full reopening of the strait conditional on US concessions, particularly as the US imposes a counter-blockade on Iranian ports. “Before any action is taken to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the United States must fully implement all the commitments it has breached,” Gharibabadi warned Washington late on Tuesday. “The Strait of Hormuz will only be reopened in exchange for an end to the war on all fronts, the lifting of the blockade and a resolution to the situation in Yemen.” Experts say such negotiations are not a quick process, as they focus on sovereignty, jurisdiction, the control of vessels and potential fees, as well as ensuring that any agreement complies with international law. “Oman and Iran are effectively negotiating elements of a post-war governance and security architecture for Hormuz — which explains the slow pace,” Omani researcher Abdallah Baaboud told AFP . For Iran, the Strait of Hormuz is also not an isolated maritime issue. Tehran links the full reopening of the strait to its standoff with Washington in the war, demanding the lifting of US sanctions, compensation for war damage and security guarantees. Oman, for its part, is seeking to “separate freedom of navigation as much as possible from the wider conflict”, with the two nations’ different strategies “the real source of the delay”, said Baaboud. What about Washington? Washington has not responded to the Iran-Oman joint statement, but beforehand it reported progress on the Hormuz issue. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly asserted that the strait is under US control — a claim denied by Tehran — and threatened Oman with bombing if the sultanate were to “stand in the way” of the US’s path through the waterway. That has put Muscat in the awkward position of trying to maintain its role as an intermediary to Tehran, without giving the impression of full support for Iranian control over Hormuz shipping for fear of risking its strategic relationship with Washington. “Washington may be uncomfortable with aspects of Oman’s diplomacy, but it also needs the channel Oman provides,” said Baaboud. By calling for other nearby coastal Gulf states to be involved in the discussions, Muscat is trying to avoid giving the impression of a one-on-one deal with Tehran, he added. The aim would be to achieve “a regional understanding in which freedom of navigation is guaranteed collectively”, rather than relying on a permanent US military presence or Iran’s ability to control the strait on its own. “That would be a very Omani outcome,” he said. “Not a grand peace settlement, but a practical arrangement that removes reasons for confrontation and opens space for wider diplomacy.”

Police said 397 officers and personnel had been deployed for the security of the main 12th Rabiul Awwal procession at Nishtar Park, and 362 more had been stationed at the entry points of the park. Karachi Additional Inspector General Azad Khan, the metropolis’s police chief, had directed law enforcers to remain on high alert on routes of all processions, and traffic police had been instructed to ensure smooth flow of traffic, the statement said.
