US designates UK-based Palestine Action as foreign 'terrorist group'. The United States on Wednesday named the UK-based Palestine Action group, which has been banned by the British government, as a “specially designated global terrorist” organisation. The US also issued sanctions against the group, claiming the move was for supporting “an act of terrorism”. Set up in 2020, Palestine Action is appealing against the UK government ban, which has led to thousands of arrests . Rights groups have decried the ban, saying it was aimed at criminalising dissent. Palestine Action had increasingly targeted Israel-linked defence companies in Britain, especially Israel’s largest defence firm Elbit Systems. Responding to the US move on Wednesday, Huda Ammori, co-founder of Palestine Action, said the group’s activities “have always been about saving lives by disrupting the Israeli war machine”. “The fact that Trump is now taking inspiration from Britain’s repression of the movement for Palestinian freedom exposes just how dangerous this ban is and should be a wake-up call to anyone who cares about free speech and civil liberties,” Ammori said in a statement to Reuters . Palestine Action’s stated goal on its website is to end “global participation in Israel’s genocidal and apartheid regime”. It gained visibility after Israel launched a devastating military onslaught on Gaza following the Oct 7, 2023 attack by fighters from Palestinian group Hamas in southern Israel. Since coming to power for his second term, US President Donald Trump has issued orders for his government to designate what it terms “far-left” groups as terrorist organisations. Wednesday’s US action also designated Italy-based Autistici/Inventati (also known as A/I Collective) as a “terrorist” organisation. The US Treasury Department also imposed sanctions on the transnational group Masar Badil, saying it operates as a front for the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine. The latter group had already been designated by the US as a Foreign Terrorist Organisation. US State Department spokesperson Tommy Piggot declared all three groups, including Palestine Action, as being “violent far-left terrorist groups”. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington would bring “the full weight of our economic tools to bear” against far-left groups. “Political terrorism has no place in our society, and we will continue to cut the financial lifelines of these groups until they are eliminated.” In April, Amnesty International declared that the leaders of the United States, Israel and Russia were seeking to impose a new “predatory” world order in their crackdowns on dissent.

Massive Nepal-Tibet flood kills 160, leaves hundreds missing. Nepali police said in an operational update on Wednesday they had recovered 157 bodies after a terrifying flood tore through the Tibet border region, taking the overall death toll to at least 160, with several hundred missing. Hundreds of tourists were still out of contact hours after the disaster hit. A torrent of mud and debris burst from the banks of a river between China and Nepal, burying buildings and triggering a frantic search for survivors. Chinese authorities said three people died and 265 others were missing after the mudslide, state media reported, citing preliminary figures from local officials. It added that President Xi Jinping ordered an “all-out” rescue effort. It was not immediately clear if there was any overlap between the Chinese figures and those announced by the Nepalese, with state broadcaster CCTV saying specific casualty figures were still being verified. “I got a call from [my brother-in-law] this morning, and they were crying and said their entire house had been swept away. Three family members were rescued, but his brother is still missing,” said 56-year-old Raju Bhadel. Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah urged the Himalayan nation to stand united after the devastating flood. “The pain and loss you have suffered is not small. But I want to assure you that you are not alone in this difficult time — the state is with you with all its means and resources,” Shah said in a statement posted to social media. “Please be patient. The government takes full responsibility for your rescue, treatment, food and shelter. In times of such a disaster, we all need to stand together.” Some 403 tourists — 341 of them foreigners — were unaccounted for several hours after the disaster struck, according to the ministry of culture, tourism and civil aviation. Nepal’s tourism board said Americans, Indians, an Australian, Malaysians and Britons were among those unaccounted for. Images shared by Nepali police showed floodwater surging through a river, sweeping away houses in its path, while AFP images depicted the top floor of a house sticking out from muddy soil. A police spokesman told AFP earlier that authorities did not know the extent of the damage but said they had “alerted people who are staying near the riverside to relocate”. The Nepal Army said it had deployed helicopters and disaster response personnel to the affected area. The Nepal Electricity Authority said about 430 megawatts of production capacity, including from hydropower and solar facilities, has been damaged. “The disaster has damaged the production, transmission and distribution facilities of the Authority… resulting in disruption of electricity supply,” it said. Sarthak Shrestha, a remote sensing and geo-information analyst at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), said a preliminary assessment showed “no anomalies” from China’s side of the border. “We believe a rock-ice avalanche occurred in Nepal, blocking the Lhende river and causing the cascading flood event,” he told AFP . Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed grief and offered his sympathies to the flood-affected people. “Deeply saddened by the loss of precious lives and widespread devastation caused by the floods and landslides in Nepal’s Rasuwa District and other affected areas,” he said in a post on X. “My heartfelt sympathies are with the bereaved families and all those affected by this tragedy. Pakistan stands in solidarity with the Government and people of Nepal during this difficult time,” he said, while praying for the safety and well-being of all those in the affected areas. Meanwhile, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar also extended condolences. “Deeply distressed by the loss of precious lives and widespread damage caused by the flash floods in Nepal. I extend my heartfelt condolences to the bereaved families, wish the injured a speedy recovery, and pray for the safe return of those still missing,” he said in an X post. “Pakistan stands firmly with the Government and people of Nepal in this difficult hour and remains ready to extend all possible assistance.” Mudslide risk Several highways were also closed, Nepali authorities said. Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported on Wednesday that “a mudslide disaster on the Nepalese side resulted in major casualties and missing people at the Gyirong Port” in Tibet. Footage shared by the broadcaster, which AFP was unable to immediately verify, showed rushing water carrying tree branches and debris, as well as a flooded road. China’s leader said that “the most urgent task is doing everything possible to search for and rescue the missing people… quickly treat injured people and minimise casualties to the greatest extent possible”, according to CCTV . Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he had spoken to Shah, and gave both his condolences and an offer to aid rescue efforts. “The people of India stand in solidarity with their sisters and brothers in Nepal at this difficult time,” Modi said in a statement. “India is ready to provide all possible humanitarian assistance to Nepal. Our teams are coordinating closely on rescue and relief efforts.” Traffic authorities in Tibet’s Shigatse said roads in the area were “at risk of mudslides and unsafe for passage” in a post on social media on Wednesday. In July last year, 17 people went missing after a mudslide near the Gyirong Port, Xinhua reported at the time. Monsoon rains from June to September regularly trigger deadly floods and landslides across South Asia. Scientists say climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events in the region. Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks at ICIMOD, said a second flood may be imminent. “With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border river, authorities warn a second flood may occur,” he told AFP .

14 infants killed in fire at Pims' gynae ward in Islamabad. ISLAMABAD: Fourteen infants were killed in a fire that broke out in the gynaecology ward of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) early on Wednesday. What has happened so far: 14 babies die after fire erupts in ward; initial reports say spark erupted from AC, blaze spread due to oxygen points Bereaved families decry rescue teams arrived “too late”; witnesses report locked doors Health secretary removed ; inquiry panel formed on PM’s orders; separate fact-finding committee constituted Health Minister Mustafa Kamal vows accountability ; Tallal Chaudhry defends district administration Condolences from across the nation, other countries pour in Footage showed rescue workers using ladders to reach broken windows to access the affected area and grief-stricken women sitting on the ground outside the hospital. An AFP reporter saw a woman in tears and a man clear glass from two broken windows, as security guards stood at the entrance to the medical facility. Several witnesses, their hands and faces blackened from the smoke, told AFP they waited hours for help from the emergency services. They were forced to smash through windows to try and get to the neonatal intensive care unit. Others said they came across locked doors and alleged guards prevented those inside the building from leaving as the fire raged. However, the hospital disputed this in a statement issued later in the evening. “All emergency exits were fully open and operational,” it asserted. In a statement, the Islamabad administration said that the fire broke out on the third floor of the Mother and Child Hospital’s ward. It said that rescue teams rushed to the scene, with six fire brigade vehicles and four ambulances taking part in the rescue operation. “The fire was immediately brought under control and the children were immediately shifted to the intensive care unit,” it said, adding that 14 children “were completely burnt”. Pims Spokesperson Dr Aneeza Jalil told Dawn that 15 babies were in the ward. “At least one baby was saved by a doctor,” she said. Health Minister Mustafa Kamal, who reached Islamabad from Karachi in the afternoon, vowed that “no one responsible for negligence, including me, will be spared”. “The tragic fire incident at Pims MCH Centre, resulting in the loss of precious neonatal lives, is deeply heartbreaking,” the public hospital said. Citing a preliminary report, the Pims statement said the incident was “initially caused by a spark inside nursery at 06:38am and within seconds a massive fire erupted due to oxygen points at each incubator”. It said two doctors and two nurses on duty inside the nursery responded “immediately and called security staff, who joined in and tried to get in twice [to bring] babies out until 06:39am, when a huge blast occurred and ceilings fell down”. The statement said the duty staff managed to rescue a baby in the nursery and four in an adjacent room, along with three mothers. “Besides immediate response, staff managed rescue of 73 other admitted patients in the adjacent Gynae ward on the same floor within minutes,” it added. The hospital asserted that “available fire safety equipment installed, including 35 fire extinguishers, were all utilised by the staff to contain the situation”. Health minister vows accountability Speaking to reporters in Islamabad, the health minister said he will present himself to his superiors for accountability. Providing details of the incident, Kamal said: “At 6:38am, it can be seen in the CCTV footage that there was a spark in the AC, then a fireball could be seen erupting out of it and landing on the floor of the ward. In one minute, at 6:39am, four people, including two nurses and two doctors, could be seen rushing for help and around the same time, the whole room was engulfed in flames”. The health minister said the incident was being investigated by “experts, different institutions including us”, adding that “nothing will remain hidden and all facts will be unearthed”. He continued: “Apparently, it seems that 14 out of the 15 infants were connected to oxygen tubes and it was that oxygen which caught flame.” Kamal reiterated that the “heart-wrenching” incident will be investigated and warned that “if there was any negligence, then as I said, we will not spare them, including myself”. The minister further said that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had instructed him “not to speak about certain issues”. He said he would be meeting the premier and that the two had been in touch. “Everyone is on board, and the findings will be presented,” he said. On being asked if he was going to tender his resignation, the health minister said, “As I have said before, whoever is responsible [..] they will not be spared. I have said what I can, and I wish I could say more, but the prime minister is my boss, and whatever his orders will be, I can only say that.” The federal minister was also questioned about fire safety standards at Pims, with a reporter pointing out that the hospital had been issued notices for the past eight years. Kamal claimed that the hospital had ensured compliance each time a notice had been issued in the past, pointing out that the blaze was contained with “26 fire extinguishers available in the building”. When a reporter asked about his early morning statement over the lack of adequate facilities at Pims and “why in his 2-2.5 years as a health minister, no improvement had been made”, the minister, getting visibly frustrated, said, “If it has been 2-2.5 years, then feel free to shoot me” and clarified that he had only been at his position for one year and two months. “What I said in the morning has to be seen within a certain parameter. I was saying that even if this did not happen, there are still challenges at the hospital. It has a capacity of 200-300 OPDs, and today, it has a footfall of over 9,000 people”. He maintained that he was merely presenting facts. “I am not saying that everything is ideal.” When pointed out that it was his responsibility to upgrade the facility, Kamal acknowledged his role and said, “We have to do it, but things cannot be ideal given the current scenario, but if we go into that, the conversation will take a different turn”. The minister reiterated that every responsible person will be held accountable. “If I am willing to present myself for accountability, then no one else is left. “Wherever there has been negligence, we will fix it,” he said. Noting that such an incident should not have happened, he said: “Will get to its root cause and ensure prevention in the future.” The minister was also asked about reports that the door of the ward was locked, to which he said that access to the ward was limited and guarded due to “instances of people stealing newborn babies a couple of years back”. “You would not see that anywhere else in the world, but we have the issue, so the door had to be manned with a guard,” Kamal explained. During his media talk, the minister got into a verbal altercation with an individual who asked when action would be taken against those responsible. As the individual got louder, the minister repeatedly gestured to him to come forward and said, “Sir, come here and talk to me.” ‘Give me my child back’ Malik Israr, whose niece was admitted to the gynae ward, told Dawn that it was unfortunate the nursery was housed in a building in which repair and renovation work was ongoing. “After the fire erupted, they told patients to vacate the building. Women who had just given birth had to rush down the stairs from the second floor,” he said. A worker removes broken pieces of a glass window after a fire broke out at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences hospital in Islamabad on Aug 26, 2026. — Reuters Khurram Mehmood, 40, told AFP he lost his three-day-old daughter in the blaze and that rescuers took hours to arrive. “I lost my daughter. She was only three days old,” he said. “My wife was in the ward. They took everyone out. We were sitting on the road waiting for help.” He added, “The fire erupted at 6am, rescue and authorities reached at 9am; people were helping themselves.” “Give me my child back,” Jaweria, who lost her newborn, said outside the hospital. “I want justice.” She told AFP : “Rescue teams arrived too late. Police arrived after four hours and said they are here to investigate. To hell with you, rescue team and police. Babies burnt to death there, but nobody could save them.” A grieving father reacts as his child’s coffin is transported in an ambulance following a fire outside the Mother and Child Health (MCH) ward at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) Hospital in Islamabad on August 26, 2026. — AFP “For two hours I kept crying and wailing,” the mother said, questioning the action taken by hospital staff and emergency responders. “Why did the doctors leave the children there? One nurse, one doctor, one gynaecologist, one paediatrician — there was nobody in the entire ward. Why were they not there?” Mudasir, another parent who also lost his child, said all doors of the ward, except one, were shut and that there was “no fire security” in the ward. A mother with black residue from the smoke on her hands stood crying outside the hospital as she held her 10-day-old baby in her arms. “People were screaming. There was black smoke. We ran for our lives. Thank god my baby is safe,” Shagufta Parveen told AFP . A man consoles a grieving father (C) as his child’s coffin is carried after a fire outside the Mother and Child Health (MCH) ward at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) hospital in Islamabad on Aug 26, 2026. — AFP Ali Abbas, 20, was with his sister who was a patient in the ward. “There was a short circuit in the nursery, in the children’s ward,” he said. “It was full of smoke.” Eyewitness Abdul Ghafoor told AFP that there was “thick black smoke inside and patients were trapped”. “I barged in to try to save as many people as I could, but we could not reach the ward where the patients were. “The fire was in the nursing room, and we could not see anything. Some of us broke the windows to help people get out.” Among the victims were the twin daughters of Bahadur Khan, a vegetable seller, The New York Times reported . He had left them with their mother to get some rest at home. Bahadur said his wife was recovering in Pims’ intensive care unit and was not aware of the deaths of their three-day-old daughters. Alam Zaib, the father of a newborn child who was in another ward and remained safe, was quoted as saying that he tried to enter the ward where the fire broke out, but the door was locked. Pims, established in 1985, is Islamabad’s biggest public sector hospital. It is one of the oldest health facilities in the federal capital and comprises several hospitals and teaching institutes. Fires in large buildings are frequent in Pakistan, often due to poor safety laws and building codes as well as lax enforcement. Health secretary removed; inquiry, fact-finding panels formed Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif took notice of the incident and directed the relevant authorities to investigate it. According to the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO), he expressed deep sorrow and grief at the incident and offered his condolences to the bereaved families. “Such a situation involving children is unbearable,” the statement quoted him as saying. “The circumstances that led to the incident should be thoroughly reviewed, those responsible should be identified, and the strictest possible action should be taken,” he said. In a second statement, the PMO said the prime minister had suspended and removed federal Health Secretary Muhammad Aslam Ghauri. The premier chaired a high-level meeting on the incident, where he expressed his anger and issued directives for “strict action”, the PMO said in another statement. It also stated that the prime minister suspended the federal health secretary and asked him to leave the meeting. The statement quoted the prime minister as saying: “I am heartbroken at this tragic incident and share the parents’ grief.” Subsequently, Captain (retired) Muhammad Mahmood, a BS-21 officer of the Pakistan Administrative Service (PAS), was appointed to the post of health secretary for three months “or till the posting of a regular incumbent,” a notification issued by the Cabinet Secretariat said. According to the PMO, a high-level inquiry committee, headed by former interior secretary Shahid Khan, has launched an investigation. According to state-run Radio Pakistan , Major General (retired) Dr Khursheed Uttra, Establishment Division Secretary Dr Barrister Nabeel Awan and Islamabad Deputy Commissioner Irfan Nawaz Memon will serve as its members. The inquiry committee will submit an interim report to the prime minister within 48 hours, containing recommendations for immediate action. It will submit a comprehensive report within five days, containing the findings of the complete investigation and actionable recommendations. The health ministry has been directed to immediately notify the inquiry committee and provide it with the necessary assistance. According to the terms of reference (ToRs), the panel will ascertain the cause of the fire and review the rescue operations carried out by the hospital staff and relevant agencies such as Rescue 1122. Besides conducting a detailed review of the fire safety infrastructure at Pims, the committee will also determine the responsibility and negligence, if any, of individuals involved in the incident. It will recommend necessary reforms for Pims’s administrative system to help prevent such kind of incidents in the future. Separately, a notification issued by the Islamabad district magistrate said that a seven-member fact-finding committee, headed by the additional deputy commissioner general (ADCG), had been formed to determine the facts behind the fire. The members of the committee included the CES director general, the City police station superintendent, the assistant commissioner (Industrial Area), the director general of Capital Development Authority’s (CDA) Electrical and Mechanical wing, along with representatives from Pims and Islamabad Electric Supply Company. The committee was tasked with determining the exact cause of the fire, assessing whether adequate and functional fire-safety measures were in place, and evaluating the response time and effectiveness of the rescue and fire-fighting operations. The notification said that a report would be furnished within 24 hours. Ambulances are parked outside a mortuary following a deadly fire at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences hospital in Islamabad on August 26, 2026. — AFP Minister of State for Law Barrister Aqeel Malik assured in a post on X that a “complete, transparent, and impartial investigation of the incident will be conducted to determine the true causes of this catastrophe and any possible negligence”. “In the event that negligence or failure is proven at any level, strict action will be taken against the responsible individuals in accordance with the law,” he added, extending his condolences to the bereaved families and expressing grief over the incident. Meanwhile, PPP leader Nayyar Hussain Bokhari, who reached Pims along with Senator Sherry Rehman and others, demanded that the head of the MCH be removed. Bokhari said it was not just negligence but rather criminal negligence and should not be ignored. Rehman said the Pims’ executive director must “answer why the system here keeps being akin to gross negligence”. “The health ministry now has no justification for taking public funds. It should be dissolved or devolved to the provinces,” she was quoted as saying by her party. She insisted they were not visiting “to play politics” but were sent by the party leadership to raise questions on behalf of the public. In a post on her X account, Rehman also shared a video of her visiting the ward. “Totally gutted. People had to break windows and jump out. Emergency gate was closed, fire equipment not working, medical staff not present,” she wrote. “Honestly, I would have resigned on the spot,” Rehman added later. Tallal Chaudhry defends district administration Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry insisted that there had not been any delay in the arrival of rescue teams and defended the district administration. “After receiving information in the control room, they reached the hospital within six minutes,” the state minister said while speaking to the media in Islamabad. He added that once the rescue teams assessed the situation, 19 people were rescued, including seven children, 1o mothers and two men. He also said that administration officials “from the assistant commissioner to commissioner to the Islamabad IG” reached the hospital to monitor the situation. “Not only did they monitor but also assisted in the rescue operation,” he said. Reiterating that rescue teams reached the site within six minutes, the state minister said, “There appears to be no negligence on the part of rescue services.” However, he added, only the hospital administration could answer for the arrangements present within the hospital. Chaudhry said that the bodies of all 14 infants had been handed over to their families. He added that a report of the incident had been sent to the prime minister and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who he said had been monitoring the situation. On being asked if Pims met the CDA’s fire safety protocols, with a journalist also pointing out that his ministry had been issuing notices to the hospital for the past seven years, he acknowledged that notices had been issued. “It is a huge institution, and notices were issued […] but what was complied with and what was not — as there are multiple buildings; we cannot conclude anything today, and an inquiry committee has been formed”. Asked why the administration had not been active on the fire safety issue before, he said, “If there has been any negligence, the inquiry committee will find out.” An inquiry committee has been formed for a “high-powered” investigation into the incident, Chaudhry noted. He said the committee will collect evidence — CCTV footage, presence of flammable equipment, why the door was locked, the number of doctors and nurses present — and present its findings. In its update on the incident, CDA said fire and rescue teams reached the site within seven minutes after a call was received at 6:54am. Fire tenders, rescue teams, ambulances of the Capital Emergency Services (CES) and the Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT) administration were part of the deployed resources. Nation expresses grief President Asif Ali Zardari expressed heartfelt condolences and sympathy to the bereaved families. In a statement, the president said that the loss of lives was “heartbreaking and an irreparable loss”. “Responsibility for the incident should be determined and action should be taken in accordance with the law,” he said. Effective fire safety and emergency arrangements must be ensured in hospitals for the protection of patients, especially newborn babies, the president urged. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said he was deeply saddened by the incident. “My deepest condolences to the bereaved parents and families. No words can ease the pain of losing an innocent child. May Allah Almighty grant the families strength and sabr in this unimaginably difficult hour,” he said. As per the prime minister’s orders an immediate and thorough investigation will establish the causes of this tragic incident to ensure that those found responsible face the strictest action. The safety of our children must remain paramount,” he said. PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari wrote on X: “Mothers do not keep their children in the womb for nine months just so that, due to someone’s negligence, they burn alive as soon as they are born. “The deaths of 14 newborns in the federal capital are one of the most horrific tragedies in human history. The helpless fathers, whose lamps of hope were extinguished the very instant they were lit, are seeking justice.” In a statement earlier in the day, he described the incident as an “unbearable tragedy for the entire nation”. He called for an impartial investigation into the incident and said the nation be informed how such a tragedy occurred at a major hospital. “Those responsible for negligence or failing to ensure the safety of patients must be held accountable,” he added, stressing that the federal government must ensure the safety of patients and medical staff at all hospitals under its administration. First Lady and MNA Aseefa Bhutto-Zardari also expressed “profound grief and sorrow over the tragic loss of newborn babies” and conveyed her “deepest sympathies to the bereaved families”. “The loss of innocent newborn lives is heartbreaking and deeply distressing,” a statement by the Presidency quoted her as saying. She called for a “thorough, swift and transparent investigation” into the incident. PML-N President Nawaz Sharif said he was “deeply grieved” to hear about the deaths. He urged the government to take strict action against those responsible and ensure measures were put in place to prevent such incidents in the future. Senate Chairman Syed Yousuf Raza Gilani expressed deep grief and sorrow over the tragic incident. In a statement, he offered his condolences to the families affected. He said effective safety measures, fire safety systems and all necessary arrangements to deal with emergencies must be ensured in hospitals to prevent such incidents. “Any negligence in safety measures is unacceptable,” he said. Gilani urged the relevant authorities to conduct a comprehensive investigation into the incident and take effective and practical steps to prevent such tragedies in the future. National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq also expressed profound grief and sorrow over the deaths of the infants. In a statement, he said he was “heartbroken” over the incident and shared equally in the pain and grief of the bereaved parents. United Nations International Children’s Emergency Fund (Unicef) called for an urgent review as it expressed grief over the incident. “Unicef is deeply saddened by the tragic loss of at least 14 newborn lives following a fire at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences hospital in Islamabad today. “We extend our deepest condolences to the bereaved families and all those affected by this devastating incident,” it said in a statement. The UN agency added, “ Every newborn deserves a safe start to life, and every mother and child should be able to receive care in a safe, secure health facility. It called for the urgent review and strengthening of fire prevention and safety standards across health facilities. The British High Commission in Pakistan termed the incident “heartbreaking news”. “Our deepest condolences and thoughts are with the parents and families at this unimaginably difficult time,” it said. Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Ministry also expressed “deepest condolences and sincere sympathy” to the families of the infants and to the people and the government of Pakistan. “The kingdom expresses its solidarity with the families of the victims and stands with the government and people of Pakistan in the face of this great tragedy, wishing the Islamic Republic of Pakistan and its brotherly people security and peace,” the statement read. The Turkish embassy said it was “deeply saddened by the tragic loss of newborn lives”, “We extend our heartfelt condolences and deepest sympathies to the bereaved families. Our thoughts and prayers are with them at this profoundly painful time. May Allah grant them strength, patience and solace,” it said on X. Spain’s embassy also extended heartfelt condolences to the bereaved families. “Our thoughts are with all those affected by this heartbreaking tragedy.” The French embassy shared the sentiment, describing the incident as “deeply distressing”. “Our hearts go out to the families who lost their newborn children in the tragic fire at Pims in Islamabad. Loss of innocent lives is heartbreaking and deeply distressing. Embassy of France extends its deepest sympathies to bereaved families and everyone affected by this tragedy,” it said in its message on X. The Pakistan Medical Association (PMA) said in a statement that it was in “deep mourning” over the incident. “The association reiterates that healthcare facilities are designed to protect and restore human lives, yet administrative failure and regulatory oversight lapses have turned these institutions into danger zones,” it said. It demanded action against officials “whose failure to uphold safety codes resulted in this catastrophe”. It also demanded enforcing strict consequences so that “systemic failure serves as a decisive warning, preventing future lapses across both public and private medical facilities”. It further said that there should be immediate restructuring and public accountability of health regulatory authorities responsible for enforcing safety protocols, building codes and emergency infrastructure in hospitals. The PMA also called for “full institutional backing for the grieving parents, ensuring they receive complete legal, financial, and emotional justice”. Search for Justice (SFJ) and Children Advocacy Network (CAN) Pakistan, a collective platform of local civil society organisations working for the protection and rights of children, also expressed their deep sorrow. “The death of newborn children in a place entrusted with their treatment and care is deeply distressing and raises serious questions about safety and emergency preparedness,” said Rashida Qureshi, programme manager at SFJ and spokesperson for CAN Pakistan. In its statement, the Islamabad Citizens Network (ICN) said, “This is not merely an unfortunate accident; it is a national tragedy in which innocent newborns, entirely dependent on the hospital system, its staff and state-provided arrangements for their safety and survival, lost their lives.” It contended that an inquiry committee headed by an ADC was “neither adequate nor appropriate given the gravity of the tragedy and the need to determine possible administrative, criminal and institutional responsibility”. ICN demanded an immediate judicial inquiry and an independent investigation into allegations by parents regarding the absence of staff, emergency exits and other administrative lapses. It recalled that similar tragic incidents had occurred in Lahore’s Services Hospital in June 2012, the National Institute of Child Health (NICH) in Karachi in January 2020, and the nursery of Sahiwal Teaching Hospital in June 2024. Civil Society Network Pakistan (CSNP) called upon Federal Constitution Court’s (FCC) Chief Justice Aminuddin Khan to take immediate notice on a suo motu basis or initiate appropriate constitutional proceedings on serious human rights violations arising out of the babies’ deaths. CSNP President Advocate Abdullah Malik told Dawn that he has also requested the FCC chief justice to consider constituting a high-level, independent and transparent inquiry to determine the exact cause and circumstances of the fire at Pims. Additional input from AFP, Reuters and Nasir Iqbal

SBP mulls ending Rs10 note on rising costs. ISLAMABAD: The State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) is considering phasing out the Rs10 banknote due to rising printing costs, while a new design for the Rs5,000 note is being prepared to curb counterfeiting. The disclosure came from Deputy Governor Dr Inayat Hussain, who briefed the Senate Standing Committee on Finance and Revenue. He said the redesigned Rs5,000 note would help reduce the circulation of counterfeit currency. The committee meeting, chaired by Senator Saleem Mandviwalla, also discussed currency security, the Pakistan Remittance Initiative, protection of foreign investments and complaints about fraudulent practices by companies. Plans new Rs5,000 note to curb counterfeiting Dr Hussain said denomination changes could follow the introduction of new currency notes. On counterfeit currency, Senator Mandviwalla told the deputy governor that he had submitted Rs5,000 notes to the SBP for verification nearly two years ago, but the bank’s response was still awaited. Responding to the query, Dr Hussain said the existing Rs5,000 note was introduced in 2005 and advances in technology had made counterfeiting easier. He said a tender had been floated under procurement rules for designing the new note. “Four bidders participated in the process and the contract was awarded to a consultant firm, which is currently incorporating the required changes,” he said, adding that the design would subsequently require federal government approval. Senator Mandviwalla directed the SBP to provide complete details of the bidding process for the redesigned Rs5,000 note, expressing concern over the circulation of counterfeit currency. Dr Hussain informed the committee that it could take about a year to introduce the new notes into circulation. He added that printing a Rs5,000 note cost around Rs14. During the meeting, Senator Anusha Rahman stressed the need to streamline the approval process for currency designs, warning against repeated referrals for minor amendments that caused unnecessary delays. Earlier this year, the committee was told that new-design banknotes with enhanced security features had been finalised by the SBP and forwarded to the federal cabinet for approval. Remittance initiative The SBP also briefed the committee on the Pakistan Remittance Initiative (PRI), saying the government had initially provided subsidies to banks to facilitate remittances by overseas Pakistanis. The committee was told that Rs120 billion had been provided as subsidy, which was curtailed during the previous year. Due to fiscal constraints, the government was unable to continue the subsidy under the current budget. Banks had therefore decided to bear the associated costs from their own resources to ensure continued facilitation of remittances. The committee appreciated the initiative and decided to invite selected banks to its next meeting to brief members on their performance and contribution to the remittance sector. Foreign investment protection The committee also reviewed the F.E. Circular, 1999, concerning the protection of investments and deposits of foreign investors in Pakistan. Dr Hussain informed the committee that instructions had been issued to concerned banks at the time to protect foreign investors’ funds and that, according to SBP records, no such case remained pending with the central bank. However, the committee expressed concern over reports that some cases involving foreign investors were still pending and sought a detailed statement on such cases, if any, including their status and reasons for delay. Senator Talha Mehmood expressed concern over companies operating in Pakistan that, despite reporting losses, may allegedly engage in fraudulent practices and mislead investors and shareholders about their financial position. He said some companies could eventually collapse or leave the country, causing financial losses to shareholders and the public. He urged the government and relevant regulators to scrutinise such companies and take timely action against fraudulent practices to safeguard public investments. Senators Sherry Rehman, Muhammad Abdul Qadir, Amir Waliuddin Chishti and Shahzaib Durrani also attended the meeting. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

Performance standards for distribution companies notified. ISLAMABAD: After more than two decades, the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) has notified sweeping guaranteed performance and overall performance standards for all distribution companies (Discos) to ensure compliance even after going into private hands under the ongoing privatisation process. The new Performance Standards (Distribution) Regulations 2026, issued by the regulator after almost two years of consultations with stakeholders, replace the Discos Performance Rules 2005. Under the new standards, utilities will, for the first time, face mandatory consumer compensation, besides heavy fines, if they fail to meet strict deadlines for restoring power after blackouts, replacing faulty meters, addressing voltage fluctuations, providing new connections and other services. Importantly, these standards establish clearer and more measurable key performance indicators (KPIs) against which the performance of distribution companies would be assessed. This is particularly important ahead of the privatisation process, as prospective investors look for clarity on the regulatory benchmarks and KPIs against which the performance of Discos would be evaluated. The new standards require complaint centres at the circle level going upto Discos management instead of relying solely on the existing centralised network. Discos will also be required to conduct biannual consumer satisfaction surveys with an accuracy rate of up to 98pc. Distribution firms face mandatory consumer compensation and fines for service failures The newly released 68-page regulatory document signals a massive shift toward consumer protection, safety requirements and power supply quality. It forces historically slow-moving monopolies to operate with unprecedented speed and transparency. All Discos would be required to create Consumer Facilitation Applications (CFAs) for direct and instant communication channel with consumers. For planned outages, Discos must give consumers 48-hour advance notice via SMS, email or other digital platforms. Defence establishments would continue to be completely exempt from unilateral power cuts. Power shutdowns to these vital installations can now only occur through mutual and prior agreements. For unscheduled outages affecting high-load industrial consumers and CPPs, utilities must give 30-minute advance warnings and provide real-time restoration updates. The only exception to this rule is a certified grid emergency. Even then, the utility must log the crisis immediately into an automated Outage Management System and report it directly to the regulator in quarterly filings. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

Little to celebrate. BY now it has become almost tedious to read the same assessment from every global credit rating agency and lender — Pakistan’s economy has stabilised, but risks remain. Moody’s commentary on the country’s economy accompanying its latest upgrade is simply a repetition of this review dressed up in a new number. And that tedium is itself the story: an economy that keeps producing the same verdict year after year is hardly holding steady; in fact, it is stuck. Macroeconomic indicators may not be falling, but nothing underneath them is moving either. Standing still while the rest of the world advances is nothing but a quiet form of decline. Moody’s new rating, still highly speculative and seven notches below investment grade, is not a vote of confidence. It is merely an acknowledgment that the country is marginally less likely to default than before. And yet it was an occasion for the prime minister to congratulate the nation as though we had turned the corner. This is the peculiar place Pakistani policymaking has settled into, where even minor technical adjustments are treated as milestones. The picture Moody’s has painted is unflattering. It points to a narrow export base, negligible FDI, heavy reliance on remittances, and a government that still leans on official and commercial borrowing to meet its external obligations. None of this describes an economy capable of standing on its own feet. It is being propped up by the IMF and rolled over bilateral deposits. The governance language deserves more attention. The agency is blunt: weak rule of law, poor control of corruption, limited government effectiveness. These are not casual observations. These are the reasons investors continue to look elsewhere. Even the improvement in debt affordability that Moody’s highlights comes with a caveat. Interest payments have reduced substantially over the previous year. Yet the figure is so high that practically nothing is left for the social and infrastructure investment the country needs. This improvement is a function of falling inflation and rate cuts, not any structural change. What all of these add up to is an economy that has been stabilised in the technical sense but the deeper conditions for real growth remain elusive. Real recovery would have looked different. Moody’s upgrade is not a turning point; it is just a slightly better seat in the same waiting room. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

Search for meaning. EACH age has brought its own set of unique challenges. The present epoch is no different, as immense technological advances go hand in hand with widespread war, uncertainty and anxiety. We are witnessing the rise of machines with mind-boggling capabilities — superintelligence, they call it — while at the same time people seem to be losing their humanity, as the arrogant and the powerful bomb and maim innocent children, without facing accountability. We ask each other: what will tomorrow bring, what world will our children inherit? These anxieties are not limited to any one country, religion or race. It seems that most of humanity — at least ordinary people who have no role in perpetuating this bloodshed and chaos — is deeply concerned about what the future holds. Perhaps in these troubled times, when materialistic philosophies fail to offer any satisfactory explanations, the message that the Holy Prophet (PBUH), whose birth we celebrate, brought over 14 centuries ago soothes the nerves and gives us some perspective: this world is transient, full of trials, and we will be made to answer for our deeds in the Divine court. This, arguably, is the core of the Quranic message and the Prophet’s Sunnah, and the crux of the message brought by all previous prophets. It explains that if the tyrants of today who spread chaos across the earth escape justice in this world, they will surely be brought before the Almighty tomorrow to answer for their crimes. As a hadith states, “the heavens and the earth stand upright by justice”. In the Noble Prophet’s life, we find examples of how to bring order to our personal and spiritual lives, as well as how to address society’s challenges. His message covered war and peace, periods of adversity and ease, how to live in the world and prepare for the hereafter. Regarding the transient nature of the world, Hazrat Ali relates that the Holy Prophet “took only that which he absolutely required from this world…”. This indicates that at all times — especially in these times of economic precarity — moderation and abstinence can help us weather the storm, as opposed to insatiable greed and the desire for more. Believers are patient in adversity. In another hadith, the Noble Prophet is reported to have said: “My Lord has commanded me to be generous and do good and He has forbidden me from being stingy and from oppressing others.” This itself is a complete remedy to address society’s ills, as it emphasises helping others, doing the right thing and resisting oppression. This ties up perfectly with another tradition attributed to Hazrat Ali, where he says that “…whenever a destitute remains hungry, it is because some rich person has denied him his share”. These noble sayings point to the deadly sins — greed; oppression; injustice — that afflict our society, as well as the world at large. Some are power drunk, attacking others and threatening to lay to waste entire civilisations. In fact, their arrogant pronouncements echo the words of the tyrants the Quran has cited, such as pharaoh, Haman and Nimrood. Elsewhere, in societies like ours, which wear the outer garb of religion, the spiritual message of the Quran can hardly be found, as the weak and the oppressed continue to cry out for justice. Whether it is tyranny across the oceans, or turmoil within ourselves and our environs, if we refer to the hadith that states that “the world is the sowing field of the Hereafter”, things start to make sense. For example, if we ‘sow’ good deeds in this world — looking out for others, helping the weak and the voiceless, honouring the rights of God and man — we will ‘reap’ eternal peace in the next world. Conver­sely, and this brings comfort to victims of injustice, those who sow chaos on the earth will reap the harvest of their evil deeds in the world to come. In these times of uncertainty and immense global upheaval, it seems that patience (sabr) holds the key to success. After all, in the Holy Quran it is stated that “Allah is with the patient” (2:153). Meanwhile in hadith, those who bear afflictions with sabr are given glad tidings. But patience/sabr does not mean accepting injustice. As people of knowledge point out, it means rejecting all forms of oppression, staying the course and bearing internal and external hardships with fortitude. During his own blessed life, the Holy Prophet faced many different kinds of adverse circumstances, from the initial days of his mission in Makkah to the establishment of a state in Madina. But he dealt with all these challenges with help from the Divine, and immense strength of character. Therefore, the message is clear for believers; as the hadith states, they are grateful in prosperity, and patient in adversity. This formula can bring meaning to those searching for a direction in these times of trial. The writer is a member of staff. Published in Dawn, August 26th, 2026

Hike in flour, onion prices adds to consumers’ woes in Karachi. • Flour millers raise prices by up to Rs275 per 50kg bag • Naan, sheermal and taftaan rates shoot up by Rs5-10 KARACHI: Ahead of the arrival of one million tonnes of imported wheat, a fresh surge in flour prices has further pushed up the rates of various varieties of roti by Rs5-10 per piece in the metropolis. Besides, consumers are facing another shock, paying Rs150-180 per kilogramme for onions, depending on their size, compared with Rs110-150 per kg a week ago. In the last week of July, onions were selling at Rs90-120 per kg. As for flour varieties, two days ago, flour millers in Karachi raised the prices of a 50kg bag of flour no. 2.5, a 50kg bag of maida and a 50kg bag of fine flour to Rs7,200, Rs7,600 and Rs7,750, respectively, an increase of Rs250-275 per 50kg bag, citing rising wheat prices in the open market. At the end of April 2026, a 50kg bag of flour no. 2.5, a 50kg bag of maida and a 50kg bag of fine flour were available at Rs5,600, Rs5,800 and Rs6,000, respectively. Following the increase in flour prices, several big tandoor operators are charging up to Rs35 for one naan, compared with Rs30, while pushing up the price of sheermal and taftaan to Rs110 from Rs100 per piece, claiming higher weight and better quality. Those who were selling naan and sheermal at Rs25 and Rs90 are now demanding Rs30 and Rs100, respectively. The Karachi commissioner had fixed in February the prices of chapati and tandoori naan weighing 120 grammes, 140, 150 grammes and 180 grammes at Rs14, Rs18, Rs21 and Rs27, respectively. In May and June, tandoor owners, while defying the official rates, had increased the prices of various varieties, including chapati roti, naan, sheermal, taftaan and kulcha, by Rs2-10 per piece, suggesting that the official rates carry little weight with the tandoor operators. Consumers have not shown any resistance to the tandoor operators pushing up the rates of roti varieties. They simply pay the inflated prices without bothering to check the weight of the dough, especially for naan. Flour prices have also gone up across the country. According to data from the Sensitive Price Index (SPI) for the week ending Aug 20, 2026, the national average price of a 20kg flour bag, a 10kg wheat bag and one kilogramme of fine flour stood at Rs2,200-3,133, Rs1,236 and Rs153, respectively, compared with Rs1,810-2,740, Rs1,039 and Rs137 at the end of March 2026. Branded flour already sells at higher rates than the normal market price. For example, a branded five-kilogramme bag of fine flour in Karachi is sold at Rs850-900, but the price regulator has taken no action. ‘Country needs over four million tonnes of wheat’ The Trading Corporation of Pakistan (TCP) has been tasked with importing one million tonnes of wheat despite a 4.3 per cent increase in wheat production during FY26 to 29.61 million tonnes, according to the Economic Survey FY26. Karachi Wholesalers Grocers Association (KWGA) chairman Rauf Ibrahim said only seven to eight months remained before the arrival of the new wheat crop, but the TCP was yet to issue an international tender for the grain import, which would take two to three months to arrive. The government should not import wheat through the TCP or commercial importers, he said, urging it to allow flour millers to import the grain themselves and fix quotas for each mill. Besides, he said, imports of one million tonnes were not enough to meet wheat and flour demand for the upcoming months. The country, he added, needed more than four million tonnes. Mr Ibrahim said there should be no ban on the inter-provincial movement of wheat. Punjab has produced 22 million tonnes this year against its consumption of 15 million tonnes, but the province has banned the movement of wheat, pushing its price in the open market to Rs130 per kg. He urged the government to resolve the wheat crisis immediately as winter demand increased, which may create a supply-demand gap and lead to further increases in the prices of various flour varieties. New onion crop to reach by end of September, October Falahi Anjuman Wholesale Vegetable Market, Super Highway, president Haji Shahjehan said only the Balochistan crop was currently feeding the entire country, while Sindh’s new crop would reach the markets by the end of September and October. Onions from Afghanistan used to help meet the supply-demand gap in the local crop, but the arrival of Afghan onions had been suspended for months. Otherwise, the situation would have been different, he said. He added that a very small quantity of onions had started arriving from Iran, but the quality was mediocre. Religious freedom panel urges sanctions against India's RSS during chief's US visit. A United States panel on religious freedom has expressed concern about a visit to the country by the chief of the Hindu nationalist group that is the ideological parent of India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), and urged sanctions on the group’s members. Mohan Bhagwat, chief of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), is on a US visit and is scheduled to speak at a Saturday event in New York City. The RSS, a powerful Hindu group from which Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s BJP emerged, said in May it had organised foreign visits to counter perceptions it is a paramilitary outfit involved in attacks on minorities. “We urge the US government to consider targeted sanctions against RSS members and Indian officials complicit in religious freedom violations, including revoking the visa issued to Mohan Bhagwat,” Asif Mahmood, chair of the US Commission on International Religious Freedom, said in a statement on Wednesday. USCIRF is a bipartisan body of the US government that monitors religious freedom around the world and makes policy recommendations, which are not binding. Washington has not imposed sanctions after recent recommendations. India’s foreign ministry has dismissed the panel’s assertions, casting USCIRF as biased against India. Rights groups say the RSS promotes majoritarian ideology fueling intolerance towards minorities. The RSS disputes being intolerant and says it is a “Hindu-centric civilisational, cultural movement” that wants to take India “to the pinnacle of glory,” including by uniting Hindus. UN and human rights groups say abuse of Indian minorities has risen in recent years. They point to rising hate speech, a religion-based citizenship law, the demolition of Muslim-owned properties, the removal of occupied Kashmir’s autonomy and an anti-conversion legislation that challenges freedom of belief. India’s BJP-led government denies being discriminatory and says its policies, including food subsidy programs and electrification drives, benefit all communities.

Qatar PM to visit Tehran to pursue US-Iran mediation efforts. Qatar’s prime minister will visit Tehran on Thursday in an effort to relaunch diplomacy after the United States and Iran traded recriminations over Washington’s promise to increase economic pressure on Tehran by targeting its trade partners for sanctions. Qatar, a Gulf neighbour of Iran and a US ally, has served as a back-channel negotiator for the warring parties and played a direct role in securing the June ceasefire that briefly led to a cessation of hostilities. The visit comes as the war nears its sixth month with fighting largely paused but no diplomatic breakthrough in sight. The two sides remain at odds over control of the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint for global oil supplies that Tehran has used as leverage. It also comes after similar visits by Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir and Omani Foreign Minister Badr Al-Busaidi. The Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) broke down in part because of differences over the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman where one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies passed before the war began on February 28. The guns have gone mostly silent the US military’s Central Command has not reported any attacks on Iran for nearly a month. Washington appears to be leaning more on economic pressure by announcing plans to cut Iran off from its trading partners with increased sanctions. Hormuz oil flows have fallen to a three-month low, with just 5 million barrels per day transiting on Monday, according to the latest ship-tracking data. Before the war, the strait carried roughly 20 million barrels per day of crude oil. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday that Iran and Oman had agreed how to share the waterway and its revenues, but a senior Iranian source later said the two countries were still working on the details of an agreement. Despite an aerial bombardment earlier in the war that severely diminished Iran’s conventional forces, Tehran has maintained enough missile and drone capability to attack Gulf neighbours that house US military bases and disrupt oil tankers in the strait. The UN’s International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has reported 70 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz since February 28 that have killed 19 seafarers. Thousands of others have died, mostly in Iran and Lebanon , since the US and Israel attacked Iran with the stated goals of denying Iran a nuclear weapon, helping Iranians topple their government, and destroying Iran’s missile programme. Mediator Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman al-Thani will discuss the continuation of Qatar’s mediation efforts and other developments in the region during his visit to Tehran on Thursday, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said. Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson said on X that Sheikh Mohammed would also address freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the need to return to the status quo before February 28, while also discussing with Iranian officials ways to “de-escalate tensions and create the conditions conducive to dialogue”. The international waterway was open to free navigation before the war, but Iran has since clung to its control of the strait as leverage and a revenue source, seeking to charge ships a commission, which the US has opposed. “An agreement with Oman over the Strait of Hormuz has not been finalised,” a senior Iranian source told Reuters , adding that the talks were continuing on the details of an accord. That seemed to contradict a statement by Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), who said Iran and Oman had “reached results that are acceptable to both sides” on controlling the strait and its revenues. Mohebbi said the strait would remain shut unless the US met Tehran’s conditions under the interim ceasefire, or memorandum of understanding, that the two sides signed in June before it unravelled. Those conditions include an end to the US blockade on Iranian ports, compensation and removal of sanctions. Iran and Oman have held on-and-off talks for weeks about controlling traffic through the strait. Tehran and Washington have each tried to assert control over the channel, imposing separate blockades.

Search underway for 1,300 missing after deadly Nepal-Tibet floods. Rescue teams rushed Thursday to find more than 1,300 people missing on the Nepal-Tibet border in flash floods and landslides that killed at least 165 and swept away entire villages. A terrifying clip of surveillance video from the Chinese side of the frontier shows a massive wall of mud and debris crashing over a building several stories high on Wednesday morning, engulfing it as dozens of people ran for their lives below. The surge swept away buses and cars like they were toys. Many of the missing are foreign tourists, officials said of the disaster, which the US Geological Survey believes was caused by a glacial collapse that sent a flow of debris engulfing areas along the way. The tsunami-like rumble of water and mud struck villages and towns on the path of two rivers — Bhote Koshi and Trishuli, with Nepali police saying they had recovered 162 bodies. Another 823 people, including 579 Nepali and foreign tourists, remained out of contact in Nepal, according to the country’s disaster agency. Across the border, Chinese state media said the “mudslide disaster” at the Gyirong Port in Tibet claimed three lives while 558 people, including 260 foreigners, were still missing. Police said they expected the death toll to rise beyond 165. “This will go up, as we have resumed the search and more bodies are expected to be recovered,” police spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle told Reuters . Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah left by road for Bidur in one of the worst-affected districts of Nuwakot to assess the flood situation, his office said on social media. Raju Bhadel, 56, a businessman in Nuwakot, recounted receiving a call from his brother-in-law in distress. “They were crying and said their entire house had been swept away. Three family members were rescued, but his brother is still missing,” he said. Also at Nuwakot, teacher Manok Mishra witnessed “nine trucks being swept away by the floods including people”. This frame grab taken from video released by the Armed Police Force of Nepal on August 26, 2026 shows rescue workers carrying a person after massive floods and landslides in Rasuwa. —AFP ‘Inland tsunami’ Rescuers waded through mud and sludge to look for survivors after floodwaters buried the lower floors of multi-storey buildings. Among those hunting for their missing family members was Subash Khatani, who told AFP he was looking for his big brother. “He is among the missing from Rasuwa. That’s why we are out to search for him,” he said. Among the missing tourists from more than two dozen countries, 177 were from India, 63 were from the United States, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada. Others included tourists from Malaysia, the Netherlands, Portugal, South Africa and South Korea, Nepal’s tourism board said. Hiking company Himalayan Glacier told AFP that 47 people from a group, including two children, were missing in Nepal. “Our teams are checking hospitals where victims are coming in,” said the company’s director Sanket Pandey. The sudden rush of mud and debris was “like an inland tsunami, travelling nearly 170 kilometres down the Bhote Koshi valley into Central Nepal”, said environmental historian Ruth Gamble of La Trobe University. “It is a popular route for international tourists travelling from Kathmandu to Lhasa,” she added. “It was a huge gush of mud coming straight towards us,” said Keshav Prasad Baral, a 68-year-old survivor being treated in a Nepali hospital. “As it got closer, it kept rising higher and higher. When I saw it enter our home, I tried to grab my wife’s hand and take her to the terrace. But she was swept away by the mud.” A helicopter ferried him to safety four hours later. “My wife is still somewhere beneath the mud,” he added. “She’s gone.” Another survivor said he saved himself by clinging to a mango tree as he watched the house where he had been working disappear. Rasuwa, in the north of Nepal, was the first district to be affected. But deaths have been reported from seven Nepali districts in total as the floodwaters raged through to Chitwan in the south, on the border with India. “There is devastation everywhere we look,” said Tula Bahadur BK, a health worker in Rasuwa. “The settlements next to the river have been completely swept away. Five of my own relatives are missing.” The Nepali Army was carrying out flights and had rescued scores of people, while others living near the river in danger zones had been told to relocate. China’s leader Xi Jinping said that “the most urgent task is doing everything possible to search for and rescue the missing people”, according to CCTV . Tibet government officials mobilised nearly 800 emergency workers and 150 vehicles as well as sniffer dogs and speed boats to help the rescue efforts, China’s state-run news agency Xinhua said. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) said it was dispatching emergency supplies including blankets, first aid kits, stretchers and body bags. “Entire villages and market areas have been wiped out,” said David Fisher, the Nepal head of IFRC. The US State Department said it was sending a disaster response adviser and providing assistance of $500,000. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said details on the disaster were scant. “Nepal … is a developing country,” he said. “It doesn’t have the resources that an event like that would have in Australia, so information is difficult.” UN teams and partners were sending supplies and personnel to support affected Nepali communities, Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said. Glacial collapse The cause of the disaster was not immediately clear in the hours after it occurred early on Wednesday, but the US Geological Survey said it was a glacial collapse that caused seismic activity and the “catastrophic” downstream impacts in Nepal and Tibet. “This event was initially reported as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake,” it said. “Additional analysis of nearby seismic stations, long-period seismic waves, and satellite imagery led to the determination that the seismic event was instead a glacial collapse and debris flow, and that no earthquake had occurred.” Climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risks of glacial lake floods and glacial collapses. Residents look at a street submerged by mud following flash floods and a landslide disaster in Devighat, in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on August 26, 2026. —AFP Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), warned of the potential for a second flood. “With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border river, authorities warn a second flood may occur,” he told AFP. Many trekking companies were not running tours during the monsoon season, but there remain significant numbers of travellers, including pilgrims, in the region. Experts cautioned that a lingering blockage in a river could produce an additional flood. Among sites hit by the flood was Syabrubesi, the gateway to the popular trekking areas, as well as by pilgrims travelling to the base of Mount Kailash, a holy site for Buddhists and Hindus. Traffic authorities in Tibet’s Shigatse said roads in the area were “at risk of mudslides and unsafe for passage”. Buddhist spiritual leader the Dalai Lama said that he was praying for all those killed in devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet. “I pray for all those who have lost their lives, and offer my sympathy and heartfelt condolences to the bereaved and to all those affected by this tragedy,” he said in a statement.

11 terrorists killed in intelligence-based operations in KP, Balochistan. The state uses the term Fitna al Khawarij for the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and refers to designated Balochistan-based groups as Fitna al Hindustan to highlight India’s role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan. “In Bannu, security forces conducted an IBO against Fitna al Khawarij , killing two terrorists and recovering weapons and ammunition,” Radio Pakistan reported. In the Ladha area of South Waziristan, five Khawarij terrorists were killed during an operation, it added. Meanwhile, four terrorists belonging to Fitna al Hindustan were killed in the Sasool area of Khuzdar district, it said. “Security forces effectively targeted Fitna al Hindustan terrorists with the assistance of [a] quadcopter,” the report said. President Asif Ali Zardari paid tribute to the security forces for their successful operation, according to a statement issued by the Presidency. “The elimination of terrorist elements active with foreign support is essential for national security and lasting peace,” the president was quoted as saying. “We will rid Pakistan of the scourge of terrorism,” he said, adding that the nation took pride in the professional capabilities and successes of the security forces and law enforcement agencies. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi also paid tribute to the security forces for their successful operations against the terrorists, according to a statement issued by his ministry. He said that security forces had thwarted the terrorists’ nefarious designs by taking timely action. The minister said the nation stood united against terrorism and in solidarity with the security forces. On Aug 21, the military’s media affairs wing said security forces eliminated 49 terrorists in separate IBOs in KP and Balochistan. UEFA drops FIFA boycott threat over Infantino’s failed investor plan. MONACO (AP) — European soccer body UEFA is set to formally withdraw its threat to boycott FIFA competitions after receiving assurances Gianni Infantino’s failed World Cup sell-off plan will not be revived. UEFA’s member federations are meeting Thursday, Aug. 27, in Monaco ahead of the Champions League draw, where they are expected to end the boycott threat, a person familiar with the proposal told The Associated Press on Wednesday, Aug. 26. The person spoke on condition of anonymity because the agenda of the closed-doors meeting was confidential. Ruling out a boycott will clear six European teams to continue preparing for the FIFA Under-20 Women’s World Cup that kicks off Sept. 5 in Poland. France and Spain named their squads last week for the 24-nation tournament which risked becoming an unwanted battleground in European soccer’s pushback against Infantino’s private investor plan. England, Italy, Portugal and host Poland also will play. The United States, Brazil and Argentina also are in the lineup. FIFA welcomed the update from UEFA in a statement, adding it “strongly believes that football has the power to unite, even in challenging circumstances, and looks forward to welcoming all teams and players to Poland.” Infantino infuriated soccer leaders worldwide last month when his plan for a $20 billion subsidiary controlling FIFA commercial rights including the World Cup was revealed by British daily The Times. The spinoff was to be 20% owned by investors led by a New York fund created by Joshua Kushner, whose initial money was to pay offers of $20 million to each of FIFA's 211 member federations. They were given a mid-September deadline to accept. The FIFA president dropped his proposal within four days amid a furious backlash led by UEFA, including the boycott threat, with support from the Asian Football Confederation and North American soccer body CONCACAF. The furor was fueled by criticism of the plan and of Infantino from senior FIFA officials. UEFA then said it wanted assurances the spinoff, to be called FIFA Forward Enterprise, would not be presented in a different form. That assurance was now received, the person told the AP. The European soccer body said Aug. 1 it had no confidence in Infantino’s leadership in a clear signal it would try to stop his reelection in March next year. The next set of FIFA competition games in Europe after the Under-20s event is qualifying playoffs for the 2027 Women's World Cup scheduled Oct. 9-13. Qualifying games for the next men's World Cup do not start until 2029. FIFA election timetable FIFA previously set a Nov. 18 deadline for candidates to enter the presidential contest, four months ahead of the vote by 211 member federations in Rabat, Morocco. Infantino had seemed sure to be reelected unopposed for a fourth and final term in office through 2031 until the turmoil created by his investor plan. The 55 UEFA member federations are attending the meeting in Monaco four weeks after they united in an online call to agree the threatened boycott.

Japan’s Sumitomo Mitsui completes 30% investment in RCBC Leasing. Yuchengco-led Rizal Commercial Banking Corp. (RCBC) said Japan’s Sumitomo Mitsui Finance and Leasing Co. Ltd. (SMFL) has completed its acquisition of a 30-percent stake in RCBC Leasing and Finance Corp. (RLFC), providing fresh capital to support the financing firm’s nationwide expansion. In a disclosure to the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE) on Thursday, Aug. 27, RCBC said that since SMFL had already satisfied all requirements, including obtaining approvals and permits from the relevant authorities, RLFC is now an equity method affiliate company of SMFL. RLFC President and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Jayson L. Mendoza said the investment supports the company’s expansion plans, foreseeing growth over the next three to five years in priority sectors such as manufacturing, construction, information technology (IT), renewable energy (RE), including electric vehicles (EVs) and solar panels, healthcare, logistics, and auto leasing. “This investment positions us well for the opportunities ahead and strengthens our capabilities that will drive our business forward,” Mendoza added. For its part, the investment allows SMFL to expand its business base in the Philippines, where strong economic growth and increasing demand for financial services are expected, by integrating SMFL’s sales and management expertise with RCBC’s strong customer base and RLFC’s team structure. Japanese financial giant Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp. (SMBC) holds a 24.46-percent stake in RCBC as a partner bank in the Philippines. Through collaboration with SMBC Group and partners, SMFL is committed to further strengthening its business base in global growth markets. RLFC is using the fresh capital infused by SMFL to fund its nationwide expansion over the next five years. SMFL is one of Japan’s largest leasing and financing businesses, with a strong presence in Asia, Europe, and the United States (US). RCBC President and CEO Reggie Cariaso said the partnership between RLFC and SMFL is aligned with the bank’s growth roadmap. “By combining our expertise with SMFL’s global capabilities, we are strengthening RLFC’s foundation for expansion and positioning ourselves to capture new opportunities,” he added. - James A.
